rows.verified: HSE identifies manual handling, moving or falling objects, machinery contact, and slips or falls as leading injury causes in glass and glazing.
Glass-cutting dust and some laminated-glass cutting products can create respiratory-sensitiser exposure.
Dust and fumes in glass and glazing can contribute to long-term respiratory illness, including occupational asthma.
Local exhaust ventilation can substantially reduce exposure to dusts and fumes in glass work.
Glass-sector controls should address lifting and carrying tasks that can cause musculoskeletal injury.
Workplaces should control risks from moving, flying or falling glass and other objects.
Machinery safeguards and safe systems are needed where workers can contact moving equipment.
Housekeeping and traffic-route controls are relevant because slips, trips and same-level falls are major accident causes.
Glass risk depends on product size, breakage potential, process temperature, machinery, handling method, layout, housekeeping and worker competence.
Glass-sector evidence is process-, material-, task-, exposure- and worker-specific and is not an exact parcel-level injury or asthma probability.
Workplace health and safety requirements apply to shipbuilding, ship repair, boat building and related repair activities.
Oxygen and fuel gases used for welding and cutting on ships require specific storage and use controls.
Restricted and confined ship spaces can intensify risks from flammable gases and hot work.
Access to and work from a vessel must be safe under general workplace and health-and-safety duties.
Sufficient lighting must be provided for shipboard work, including where lighting forms part of work equipment.
Work inside boilers, tanks and similar spaces is subject to confined-space controls.
Heavy hatch beams, plates and components must be secured against falling or toppling.
Ship hot-work planning should account for gas-cylinder condition, ventilation, ignition control and emergency arrangements.
Shipbuilding risk depends on vessel condition, task, access, hot work, gas inventory, enclosure, weather, lifting plan and contractor coordination.
Ship-repair evidence is vessel-, task-, space-, gas-, equipment- and workforce-specific and is not an exact parcel-level incident probability.
